propositions.text: Credibility findings cannot be solely based on objective country conditions; key problematic non-credible findings of applicants' narrative must be considered.
propositions.quote: Credibility findings cannot be solely based on objective country conditions, without taking into account key problematic non-credible findings of a narrative of applicants, itself.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that credibility findings must consider applicants' narrative issues, not just objective country conditions.

propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of an RPD decision rejecting their refugee claim under IRPA sections 96 and 97.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act... of a decision by the Refugee Protection Division... wherein the RPD rejected the Applicants’ claim for refugee protection under sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The applicants are seeking judicial review of the RPD's rejection of their refugee claim under IRPA sections 96 and 97.

propositions.text: The applicants are Muhammad Siddique Khurram, Fatima Muhammad Khurram, Hamza Muhammad Khurram Muh, and Omar Muhammad Khurram, all Pakistani citizens.
propositions.quote: The Applicants, Muhammad Siddique Khurram [Principal Applicant] (age 36), Fatima Muhammad Khurram (age 34), Hamza Muhammad Khurram Muh (age 6) and Omar Muhammad Khurram (age 5), are citizens of Pakistan.

paragraphs.summary: The applicants are a family of four, all citizens of Pakistan.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant is Sunni, wife is Shia; they married in 2009 and lived in UAE for work.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant is a Sunni Muslim; and his wife is a Shia Muslim. They married in 2009. Upon their marriage, they returned to the United Arab Emirates [UAE] for employment purposes.

propositions.text: In October 2012, they traveled to Pakistan for son's medical treatment.
propositions.quote: The Applicants then, in October 2012, travelled to Pakistan for medical treatments for their eldest son.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant alleges he was abducted in Pakistan in November 2012 due to his marriage to a Shia Muslim.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant alleges that he was abducted because he is married to a Shia Muslim by what he believes to be members of an Islamic organization.

propositions.text: He was allegedly released after agreeing to leave a package in a Shia mosque.
propositions.quote: He was allegedly released upon accepting to leave a package inside a Shia mosque.

paragraphs.summary: The Principal Applicant (Sunni) and his wife (Shia) married, lived in UAE, traveled to Pakistan, where he alleges abduction due to inter-sect marriage.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant stated police refused to take his complaint after abduction.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant stated that he went to the police station; and, that the police officers had refused to take his complaint; and, thus, not write a report.

propositions.text: Applicants fled to Dubai on November 9, 2012, after visa denials for Canada and later traveled to UK and US.
propositions.quote: On November 9, 2012, the Applicants fled to Dubai; their applications for visas to Canada to visit the Principal Applicant’s brother were denied; and, in June 2014, they travelled to the United Kingdom for a family vacation. In January 2015, the Applicants successfully obtained visas for the United States but their applications for temporary visitors’ visas to Canada were again rejected in February 2015.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant alleges he received threatening texts in February 2015 from abductors; wife and children were victims of two intentional car accidents.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant alleges that he began to receive threatening text messages by members of the organization who had abducted him in November 2012. His wife and children had also been victims of two car accidents; which had been intentionally caused.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant did not report incidents to UAE authorities due to fear of deportation; claims incidents are related.
propositions.quote: Still, the Principal Applicant did not report these significant incidents and the text messages to the authorities in the UAE due to fear of deportation. According to the Principal Applicant the incidents are related.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege police refused complaint, fled to Dubai, received threats and suffered accidents, but did not report to UAE authorities due to deportation fears.

propositions.text: Applicants left Dubai for US on May 31, 2015, arrived in Canada June 2, 2015.
propositions.quote: On May 31, 2015, the Applicants left Dubai for the United States and arrived in Canada on June 2, 2015.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant alleges he continued to receive threatening texts in Canada but did not report to Canadian authorities.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant alleges that even while in Canada he kept receiving threatening text messages from the same individuals; but, still did not report the incidents to the Canadian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants arrived in Canada in June 2015; Principal Applicant alleges continued threats but did not report to Canadian authorities.

propositions.text: RPD found applicants not credible except for their identities and citizenships; found abduction story not plausible.
propositions.quote: the RPD held that the Applicants are not credible except for the fact that the Principal Applicant is a Sunni from Pakistan and his wife is a Shia, born and raised in the UAE, and is a citizen of Pakistan, both children are citizens of Pakistan. In essence, the RPD found that the Principal Applicant’s story of abduction is not plausible.

propositions.text: RPD found claim about police refusal to register report unsupported by documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: the Principal Applicant’s claim that the Pakistani police had refused to register a “First Information Report” is not supported by documentary evidence.

propositions.text: RPD found applicants' claim of inability to approach UAE authorities not reasonable or credible; documentary evidence does not support deportation risk due to Shia status.
propositions.quote: the Applicants contentions that they were not able to approach the UAE authorities about the alleged threats are not reasonable or credible; as both the Principal Applicant and his wife had legal resident status in the UAE; and, the documentary evidence does not support their claim of deportation simply because his wife is a Shia Muslim.

propositions.text: RPD found it implausible that Principal Applicant would not change phone number in UAE and Canada; did not believe he received threats in Canada.
propositions.quote: the RPD found that it was implausible that the Principal Applicant would not have changed his cellphone number in the UAE and in Canada simply because of his friends and due to his work. The RPD also did not believe that the Principal Applicant did receive threatening text messages while in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the applicants not credible, doubting the abduction, police refusal, inability to approach UAE authorities, and threat claims.

propositions.text: RPD found no evidence of persecution of Sunni-Shia couples or illegality/discrimination of such marriages in Pakistan.
propositions.quote: There is no reference to the targeting and persecution of Sunni Muslims who are married to Shia Muslims by extremists, other groups or any authority in Pakistan”; and, that “[t]here is no evidence to confirm that Sunni Muslim and Shia Muslim marriages are illegal or subject to discrimination let alone discrimination that would amount to persecution

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no evidence of persecution or discrimination against Sunni-Shia couples in Pakistan.

propositions.text: RPD rejected the applicants' refugee claim.
propositions.quote: the RPD rejected the Applicants refugee claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the applicants' refugee claim.

propositions.text: Issues: Did RPD misframe claim as interfaith marriage? Did RPD err in credibility findings? Did RPD fail to analyze section 97?
propositions.quote: The central issues to be determined by this application for judicial review are: 1) Did the RPD erroneously frame the claim as a fear of persecution on the basis of an interfaith marriage? 2) Did the RPD err in its credibility findings? 3) Did the RPD err by not performing a separate section 97 analysis?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies three central issues: claim framing, credibility findings, and section 97 analysis by the RPD.

propositions.text: Court sets out relevant IRPA legislative provisions for Convention refugee and person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The following are the relevant legislative provisions of the IRPA: Convention refugee Définition de “réfugié” 96. A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution...

paragraphs.summary: The court provides the relevant IRPA legislative definitions for refugee and person in need of protection.

propositions.text: RPD unreasonably rejected claim, limited analysis to mixed marriage, made unreasonable plausibility and credibility findings, misstated/ignored evidence, relied on specialized knowledge, and failed to analyze section 97.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the RPD unreasonably held that the Applicants refugee claim should be rejected. They raised several arguments to support their position. Broadly, they submit that the RPD unreasonably limited its analysis of the persecution faced by the Applicants on the basis of a mixed Sunni-Shia Muslim marriage; when in fact the claim of persecution is on the basis that the Principal Applicant’s wife is a Shia Muslim in Pakistan. Secondly, the RPD made unreasonable plausibility findings and consequently led the RPD to inaccurately hold that the Principal Applicant was not credible. Furthermore, the RPD’s credibility findings towards the Principal Applicant are unreasonable as the RPD had misstated evidence and ignored corroborating documentary evidence. Thirdly, the RPD erred by relying on specialized knowledge without affording them an adequate opportunity to respond. Finally, the RPD erred by not making a full analysis of the Applicants’ claim under section 97 of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue the RPD unreasonably rejected their claim, misframed the persecution, made unreasonable findings, and failed to analyze section 97.

propositions.text: Respondent submits RPD's negative credibility findings are reasonable; narrative lacks corroboration; no reliance on specialized knowledge; disbelief reasonable.
propositions.quote: the Respondent submits the negative credibility findings of the RPD are reasonable as the implausibility findings are reasonable; the Applicants narrative lacks corroborative evidence; the RPD did not rely on specialized knowledge; and, the RPD reasonably disbelieved the Applicants’ allegations.

propositions.text: RPD did not unduly restrict analysis; decision must be read as a whole.
propositions.quote: the RPD did not unduly restrict its analysis of the Applicants’ claim; and, the Court must read the RPD’s decision as a whole.

propositions.text: Section 96 is a lower standard; RPD did not err by rejecting claim under section 97 without reasons.
propositions.quote: since section 96 of the IRPA is based on a lower standard, the RPD did not err by rejecting the Applicants’ claim under section 97 of the IRPA without providing reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues RPD's findings are reasonable, analysis was not restricted, and section 97 reasoning was not required.

propositions.text: All three issues are reviewed for reasonableness as they involve mixed law and fact or factual findings by the RPD.
propositions.quote: All three issues before this Court must be reviewed under the standard of reasonableness as they deal with mix law and fact findings and factual findings by the RPD

paragraphs.summary: The court will review all issues under the reasonableness standard as they involve mixed law and fact or factual findings.

propositions.text: Applicants submit RPD erred by restricting claim to interfaith marriage; claim is based on wife's Shia status in Pakistan, heightened by interdenominational marriage.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the RPD erred by restricting the claim to an interfaith marriage. The claim was generally based on the fact that the Applicant’s wife is a Shia in Pakistan and that the risk of persecution was heightened by the fact that he, as a Sunni Muslim, had entered into an interdenominational marriage.

propositions.text: Court finds RPD did consider risk to Shia Muslims in Pakistan and did not unreasonably restrict analysis to interfaith marriage.
propositions.quote: The Court does not find that this is the case. At paragraph 28 of its decision, the RPD clearly considered the fact that Shia Muslims have been targeted by Sunni fundamentalist groups throughout Pakistan; and, that the UNHCR Eligibility Guidelines for Assessing the International Protection Needs of Members of Religious Minorities from Pakistan (dated 14 May 2012) states that members of the Shia community may be in need of international protection. Hence, it would be erroneous to find that the RPD unreasonably restricted its analysis of the claim to one of interfaith marriage and not to the fact that the Applicant’s wife is a Shia Muslim in Pakistan.

propositions.text: Credibility findings cannot be solely based on objective country conditions; must consider problematic non-credible findings in applicants' narrative.
propositions.quote: Credibility findings cannot be solely based on objective country conditions, without taking into account key problematic non-credible findings of a narrative of applicants, itself.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RPD misframed claim, but court finds RPD considered Shia risk; court reiterates credibility findings must consider narrative, not just country conditions.

propositions.text: RPD made negative credibility finding, holding Principal Applicant's 2012 Pakistan visit narrative was fabricated, based on several implausibility findings.
propositions.quote: the RPD held that on the balance of probabilities, the Principal Applicant’s narrative of motives and reasons for and surrounding his 2012 visit to Pakistan was fabricated. This negative credibility finding is the result of numerous implausibility findings by the RPD.

propositions.text: RPD found it implausible that: i) abduction occurred; ii) police refused report; iii) UAE authorities couldn't be approached; iv) car accidents were deliberate; v) phone number not changed after threats; vi) phone number not changed in Canada; vii) threats not reported to Canadian authorities.
propositions.quote: The RPD held that it was implausible that: i) the Principal Applicant had been abducted by an Islamic organization in Pakistan in November 2012; ii) the Pakistani police would have refused to register a First Information Report the day after the alleged abduction; iii) the Applicants were unable to approach the UAE authorities regarding the threatening text messages received by fear of deportation given that the Principal Applicant’s wife is a Shia; iv) the Principal Applicant’s wife two motor vehicle accidents having been deliberately caused; v) the Principal Applicant would not change his phone number after receiving threatening calls and text messages; vi) the Principal Applicant would not change his phone number upon his arrival in Canada; and, vii) the Principal Applicant would not report the threatening texts to the Canadian authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the Principal Applicant's narrative fabricated, listing several implausibilities regarding abduction, police, authorities, accidents, and phone behavior.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant submits RPD's adverse credibility findings are unsupported by evidence.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant submits that the RPD made adverse credibility findings that are not supported by the evidence.

propositions.text: Court owes deference to RPD's credibility findings, but implausibility must be clear and based on reliable, verifiable evidence.
propositions.quote: Great deference is owed by this Court to RPD’s assessment of the evidence and credibility findings – such as plausibility findings... the implausibility must be clear and the RPD should provide a reliable and verifiable evidentiary base against which the plausibility of the Applicant's evidence may be judged

propositions.text: RPD must consider claimant's milieu and culture in plausibility findings; what is implausible in Canada may not be elsewhere.
propositions.quote: The RPD must not make implausibility findings without regard to the claimant’s milieu and culture; as such, what might be implausible on the basis of Canadian standards may be based on the claimant’s milieu

propositions.text: Court agrees plausibility findings are needed, but must be based on significant subjective or objective evidence, which exists in this case.
propositions.quote: There is a need for plausibility findings; however, must be based on either significant subjective, or objective evidence, or both which in this case, they are.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Applicant challenges RPD's credibility findings; court explains deference, need for clear evidence, and finds plausibility findings are supported here.

propositions.text: Except for the First Information Report issue, RPD's negative plausibility findings are reasonable and supported by reliable evidence considering applicants' milieu.
propositions.quote: With the only possible exception of the negative credibility inference regarding the First Information Report, the Court is of the opinion that the RPD’s negative plausibility findings are reasonable as they are intertwined with numerous adverse credibility conclusions which are supported by reliable and a verifiable evidentiary based reasons, made with regard to the Applicants’ milieu.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's negative plausibility findings reasonable and evidence-based, except possibly regarding the First Information Report.

propositions.text: RPD's finding on lack of First Information Report is questionable, as evidence shows bribes are usually required; RPD did not probe further.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s implausibility finding regarding the lack of a registered First Information Report is, in itself, perhaps, opened to question, as the documentary evidence specified by the RPD is that the registration of a First Information Report generally requires the payment of a bribe. As the RPD did not dig deeper and did not ask the Principal Applicant as to whether he had been told to pay a bribe and as to why the Pakistani police refused to register a First Information Report, it was possible to reflect on why the RPD found that the lack of a First Information Report undermines the Applicants’ claim.

propositions.text: This one implausibility finding is not central; RPD relied on other significant evidence, so overall negative credibility finding is reasonable.
propositions.quote: Nonetheless, as this one implausibility finding, in and of itself, is not central to the overall negative credibility finding; and, given that the RPD did rely on numerous other significant elements of evidence to arrive at its conclusion, it was reasonable for the RPD to arrive at a negative finding regarding the Applicants and to disbelieve their narrative on the basis of a lack of credibility

paragraphs.summary: The court questions the RPD's First Information Report finding but finds it non-central, and overall negative credibility finding remains reasonable.

propositions.text: Court's role is not to hunt for errors line-by-line but to review the RPD decision as an organic whole.
propositions.quote: The role of the Court, in reviewing RPD’s reasons, is not to engage in a line-by-line hunt for a possible error, its role is to approach the decision as an organic whole, a sum of all parts

paragraphs.summary: The court states its review is holistic, not a line-by-line search for errors in the RPD's decision.

propositions.text: The RPD's state protection analysis applied equally to sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: As the state protection analysis of the RPD applied equally to sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA,

propositions.text: There was no need for the RPD to make a separate analysis under section 97 of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: there was no need for the RPD to make a separate analysis under section 97 of the IRPA

propositions.text: The Court is satisfied that the RPD considered the criteria applicable for each section.
propositions.quote: the Court is satisfied that the RPD considered the criteria applicable for each section

propositions.text: Karafazlioglu and Bellingy support that a separate section 97 analysis is unnecessary if the criteria are considered.
propositions.quote: Karafazlioglu v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 302 at para 13; Bellingy v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1252 at para 53

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the RPD's state protection analysis covered both sections 96 and 97, so a separate section 97 analysis was unnecessary, citing case law.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: the application for judicial review is dismissed.

propositions.text: There is no serious question of general importance to be certified.
propositions.quote: There is not serious question of general importance to be certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review and finds no serious question of general importance to certify.
